evaluated.name: EVCashYieldMinusWCBuildup
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che)), NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low enterprise multiple is attractive only if the operating profit behind it is not being generated by inflating non-cash working capital; balance-sheet accrual buildup signals that EBITDA overstates distributable cash.
evaluated.reasoning: Using EV (equity plus debt minus cash) makes the valuation leg capital-structure neutral and directly comparable to EBITDA, while the change in non-cash working capital (wcap net of cash) is the balance-sheet measure of accruals that pollutes EBITDA. Combining a high EBITDA/EV rank with a low working-capital-accrual rank targets firms that are cheap on cash-generating operations rather than on accounting-inflated operating income.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SalesYieldNonCashCurrentAssetDrag
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A low price-to-sales multiple is a bargain only when revenue is collected rather than parked in receivables and inventory; firms whose non-cash current assets balloon relative to sales are recognizing revenue that has not converted to cash.
evaluated.reasoning: The revenue-quality leg is now built from balance-sheet items with broad coverage (act, che, sale) instead of the sparse and sign-inconsistent cash-flow-statement components, and it excludes payables entirely so that stretching suppliers can no longer masquerade as high quality. Scaling the change in non-cash current assets by sales makes the two legs conceptually matched: both are per-dollar-of-revenue measures, so the composite isolates cheap firms whose revenue base is genuinely cash-converting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accounting quality is priced least efficiently inside the value tail; among cheap firms, low balance-sheet accruals identify genuine bargains and high accruals identify value traps, while among glamour firms the accrual signal carries little incremental information.
evaluated.reasoning: The bounded cheapness rank acts as a conditioning weight (near zero for expensive and negative-book-equity firms, so no sign pathology), and the signed, winsorized balance-sheet accrual z-score supplies direction, so the long-short spread is long cheap-and-clean versus short cheap-and-dirty. Because both legs sit in the value/low-price region, HML and CMA loadings largely cancel, which is exactly the structural fix for the near-zero FF5 alphas of generation 0's additive composites.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValueWithStableWorkingCapital
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(wcap, at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Erratic working capital signals opaque, hard-to-audit accounting, so investors rationally discount such firms; cheap firms with smooth working-capital intensity are more likely to be genuine mispricings whose value discount closes.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the invalidated second-moment idea using an accrual-exclusive state variable (wcap) whose five-year volatility is computable from annual balance sheets with wide coverage. It tests an information-risk mechanism rather than an accrual-level mechanism, so if the level-based composites keep getting absorbed by FF5, a dispersion-based accounting-opacity leg tells us something new about which cheap firms are traps.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValueWithNOWCAtOwnHistoryLow
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital norms differ enormously across business models, so what matters is whether a firm's non-cash working capital sits high or low relative to its own five-year history; cheap firms whose balance sheet is currently lean by their own standard have already worked off past accruals and face no reversal drag.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the discredited "linear-in-B/M" construction and replaces the cross-sectional accrual level with a within-firm time-series position (TS_RANK), which removes industry and business-model differences in normal working-capital intensity that contaminate cross-sectional accrual ranks. It is therefore mechanistically distinct from the archive's cross-sectional level, flow, and volatility legs, and it avoids negative-numerator distress artifacts because the valuation leg keeps standard book equity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DepreciationConservatismValue
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ni, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dp, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Depreciation is the largest non-discretionary negative accrual; firms that depreciate aggressively relative to industry peers understate reported earnings, so a high earnings yield achieved despite conservative accounting understates true cash profitability and is systematically underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the mirror image of the usual accrual story and is not a reconstruction of cash-flow-to-price: the signal deliberately rewards a *large* negative accrual, so it separates firms that are cheap because earnings are conservatively stated from firms that are cheap on inflated income. Industry z-scoring of dp/at is essential because depreciation intensity mostly reflects capital intensity, and it makes the accounting-conservatism component orthogonal to sector composition.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EarningsYieldAsymmetricAccrualPenalty
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ni, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(MUL(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), 0))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only income-increasing accruals carry manipulation content; working-capital releases (negative accruals) reflect operating discipline or conservatism rather than inflated earnings, so the value signal should be penalized for accrual build-ups but not symmetrically rewarded for run-downs.
evaluated.reasoning: The tax-payable leg is abandoned because, as noted, Δtxp is itself a current-liability accrual and too small and sparse to carry half the signal weight; it is replaced by a positive-part accrual penalty built with INDICATOR, which imposes an economically motivated asymmetry rather than a linear accrual rank. This isolates a specific design question the archive cannot answer: whether the value-trap effect is driven entirely by the income-increasing tail of accruals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SalesYieldReceivableGrowthDivergence
evaluated.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(act, che), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Revenue quality is revealed by whether non-cash current assets grow faster than the revenue they support; a low price-to-sales multiple is a genuine bargain only when receivables and inventory are not outrunning sales.
evaluated.reasoning: This fixes the cash-contamination flaw by explicitly excluding che from the working-capital measure, so cash accumulation no longer looks like accrual bloat, and it changes the statistic rather than the horizon: a growth-rate divergence is scale-free and directly matched to the sales-based valuation leg, unlike an asset-scaled level change. The receivables-versus-sales growth gap is the classic revenue-recognition red flag, giving a clean test of whether cheap-on-sales firms with deteriorating revenue quality are the traps.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValuePremiumGatedByCleanAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value premium exists only where reported fundamentals are trustworthy: among clean-accrual firms cheapness predicts high returns, while among accrual-inflated firms book value is unreliable and the value spread should be flat or perverse.
evaluated.reasoning: This inverts the conditioning of the archive's only alpha-positive signal — accrual quality becomes the bounded gate and signed cheapness carries direction — so the long-short spread is long cheap-clean versus short expensive-clean, holding accounting quality high in both legs. Comparing its alpha to ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual identifies whether the interaction is a value effect concentrated in clean firms or an accrual effect concentrated in cheap firms, which is the single most informative unresolved design question in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PercentAccrualGatedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), ABS(ib))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a high earnings yield is the share of that income which is accrual rather than cash, so accruals should be deflated by the magnitude of earnings, not by assets; a cheap-on-earnings firm whose income is mostly accrual is a trap regardless of its asset base.
evaluated.reasoning: Scaling accruals by absolute earnings makes the accrual leg commensurate with the earnings-yield valuation leg, so the interaction measures the reliability of the very quantity being capitalized, unlike asset-scaled accruals which mix in capital intensity. This isolates the deflator design choice against the gen-1 winner while switching the valuation channel from book-to-market to earnings yield, giving a cleaner economic reading of "cheap on earnings that are actually cash."
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValueWithGrossOperatingBalanceSheetChurn
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1), sale))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Sloan accruals net asset-side buildup against liability-side buildup, but for a cheap firm both are bad news: growing receivables and inventory signal unsold or uncollected revenue, while growing payables and accrued liabilities signal stretched suppliers and funding strain, so the two should enter with the same sign rather than opposite signs.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a decomposition test of the accrual leg itself: if the netted Sloan measure works only because of its asset side, then a gross-churn version that also penalizes operating-liability expansion should perform at least as well among value stocks and better in the distress tail. Sales scaling keeps both components commensurate with operating volume and avoids the capital-intensity contamination of asset scaling.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValueWithPersistentlyCleanAccruals
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 0), 5)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of low accruals can be luck or a one-off working-capital release; a multi-year record of income-decreasing accruals reveals a conservative reporting policy, and cheap firms with such a record are the ones whose book value can be trusted.
evaluated.reasoning: This repairs the failure of ValueWithStableWorkingCapital, whose FF5 alpha was significantly negative (−3.4%/yr, t = −3.5) partly because VOL over five annual points is a very noisy second moment and raw wcap measures cash-holding variability rather than accounting policy. Counting the number of clean-accrual years is a robust persistence statistic on a properly cash-excluded accrual measure, testing whether reporting-policy consistency, rather than accrual dispersion, is what distinguishes real value from value traps.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ValueWithWorkingCapitalOffItsPeak
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 5), RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual bloat is a state, not a flow: a cheap firm whose non-cash working-capital intensity now sits far below its own five-year peak has already absorbed and reversed its accrual excess, so its depressed earnings are the trough rather than the start of a decline, whereas a cheap firm sitting at its own peak still has the reversal ahead of it.
evaluated.reasoning: The telescoping and 1/price problems are both removed: distance-from-own-peak is a genuine level state that cannot collapse into a five-year difference, and no fundamental is divided by market cap, so the signal is not a repackaged accrual-to-price ratio. It retains the value-gated multiplicative architecture because that is the only form in the archive that produced a reliable FF5 alpha (both legs are cheap stocks so HML and CMA cancel), while the accrual content — reversal stage measured against the firm's own history — is new relative to level, gross-churn, percent, and persistence versions already queued.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DeratingWithCleanAccrualSurprise
evaluated.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(SUB(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What identifies a value trap is not a low valuation level but a *de-rating* accompanied by deteriorating accounting: when a firm becomes cheap relative to its own valuation history while its accruals rise above their own multi-year norm, the price decline is confirmation of fundamental erosion; when the same de-rating occurs with accruals below their own norm, it is sentiment-driven mispricing that reverts.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs are benchmarked to the firm's own history — a time-series cheapness position and an accrual surprise relative to its own three-year average — so the construction is industry- and business-model-free by design rather than by mechanical demeaning, and it adds new economic content (de-rating dynamics interacted with accrual deterioration) instead of re-scaling the gen-1 winner. The accrual leg is winsorized before z-scoring, fixing the outlier exposure the critic identified.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashFlowStatementAccrualGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dpc), oancf), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, the reliability of reported earnings is best measured by the wedge between income before depreciation and actual operating cash flow, because balance-sheet differences also move with acquisitions, divestitures and write-offs that have nothing to do with earnings quality.
evaluated.reasoning: Every accrual leg tested so far has been a balance-sheet delta; measuring working-capital accruals directly from the cash-flow statement (ib + dpc − oancf) removes non-articulation noise and should sharpen both the cross-sectional slope and the portfolio spread if measurement error was diluting the archive's gated signals. It keeps the cheapness gate that the evidence shows is required for FF5 alpha, so any change in performance is attributable to accrual measurement alone.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AssetSideAccrualGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value-trap effect comes from the asset side of accruals — receivables and inventory that represent revenue not yet collected or sold — while operating-liability growth is a financing/liquidity phenomenon that carries the opposite return sign.
evaluated.reasoning: The gross-churn test showed that adding operating-liability growth with a penalizing sign flips the FF5 alpha from +2.5% to −2.3%, which implies the liability side works in the opposite direction; the clean follow-up is to strip the liability side out entirely and see whether asset-side buildup alone reproduces or beats the netted Sloan measure. If it does, the mechanism is specifically about uncollected revenue and unsold inventory rather than total accrual accounting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ChronicAccrualRelianceGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of accruals is a noisy read on accounting quality; what makes a cheap firm a trap is chronic, multi-year reliance on accruals to report income, and the average accrual rate over three years measures that reliance while preserving magnitude.
evaluated.reasoning: The persistence-count repair failed (alpha −1.9%) precisely because a 0–5 count throws away how large the accruals were, so the better fix is a magnitude-preserving three-year mean, which also reduces annual re-ranking and should raise the poor Sharpe (0.20) of the gated family. If chronic accrual reliance beats the one-year measure, the mechanism is a persistent reporting-policy effect rather than a one-year reversal effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SoftBookShareGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), ceq)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Book-to-market is only trustworthy if book equity is composed of hard assets; when most of a cheap firm's equity is non-cash working capital, the denominator of its value case is soft accrual-based accounting subject to write-down, making the discount illusory.
evaluated.reasoning: This attacks the accrual stock embedded in the value ratio's own numerator rather than the annual accrual flow, so it tests bloat versus flow as the operative concept, and unlike the earlier "hard book-to-market" attempt it stays multiplicative-conditional and never creates negative or uninterpretable numerators. It requires no differencing or multi-year window, so coverage should exceed the archive's typical 0.105–0.11 and portfolio composition should be more stable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SalesDeflatedAccrualGatedEarningsYield
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), sale)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: For a firm that looks cheap on earnings, the relevant question is how much accrual accounting was needed per dollar of revenue to produce those earnings; revenue is a stable, always-positive deflator that keeps the accrual measure comparable without exploding for marginally profitable firms.
evaluated.reasoning: The earnings-yield-gated version produced the archive's most reliable alpha (2.9%, t=2.8) but a weak FMB t of 1.4, and the likely culprit is the ABS(ib) deflator, which explodes near zero earnings and creates extreme, non-monotone signal values exactly among the marginal firms; sales deflation preserves the "accrual intensity of reported profit" idea with a well-behaved scale. This isolates the deflator choice while keeping the earnings-yield gate whose alpha evidence is the strongest in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DiscretionaryWCAccrualGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 1))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all accruals are discretionary: working capital that grows in proportion to revenue is the normal cost of doing business, and industry-wide swings in receivable and inventory intensity reflect credit and demand cycles, so only the residual — a rise in working-capital-to-sales beyond the firm's revenue scale and beyond its industry's contemporaneous move — indicates earnings that were manufactured rather than earned.
evaluated.reasoning: Every accrual leg in the archive measures *total* accruals, so the untested economic question is whether the value-trap effect comes from the discretionary component; differencing the working-capital-to-sales ratio removes growth-justified accrual investment mechanically, and IND_ADJ then removes the common industry cycle, leaving a firm-specific abnormal accrual. This replaces the mechanical re-blend with a normal-versus-discretionary decomposition, and because the residual is a much cleaner manipulation proxy it should sharpen the cross-sectional slope while retaining the value-gated architecture that is the only one delivering FF5 alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ReceivableInventoryCashDrainGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(ADD(RATIO(recch, at), RATIO(invch, at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value-trap channel is specifically that revenue has been booked but not collected and goods produced but not sold, and the cash-flow statement reports these two drains directly rather than inferring them from contaminated balance-sheet differences.
evaluated.reasoning: Two separate archive results point here: cash-flow-statement measurement produced the best alpha of any accrual leg, and the gross-churn failure showed the liability side works in the opposite direction, so the natural intersection is the asset-side components measured from the cash-flow statement. Compustat reports recch and invch as cash-flow effects (positive when receivables or inventory are released), so the leg enters unnegated, and coverage is the main risk to monitor.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: PeerRelativeBloatGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working-capital bloat only signals soft accounting when it is abnormal for the firm's line of business; distributors and manufacturers require structurally high working capital, so the trap indicator is bloat relative to industry peers, scaled by total assets rather than by fragile book equity.
evaluated.reasoning: The soft-book version produced a large alpha (+4.1%) but a wrong-signed FMB t and negative Sharpe, exactly what one expects if the ratio is unstable in the distressed tail (small or negative ceq) and is partly sorting on working-capital-intensive industries. Replacing the denominator with total assets and demeaning within industry fixes both defects while keeping the stock-versus-flow question that motivated it.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EVYieldGatedAccrualQuality
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accrual quality should be evaluated conditional on how cheap the firm's operating cash-generating capacity is relative to its whole capital structure, not on book-to-market, because the enterprise multiple identifies cheapness without the leverage and write-off distortions embedded in book equity.
evaluated.reasoning: Every gated signal so far has used a price-to-book or price-to-earnings gate, which is nearly collinear with HML, so the resulting spread earns alpha mainly through negative factor loadings while its raw return stays near zero (Sharpe 0.03–0.19); the EBITDA/EV gate was the archive's best raw-return valuation leg (Sharpe 0.283). Swapping the gate isolates whether the gated family's weak Sharpe is a HML-collinearity problem rather than an accrual-measurement problem.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ConservativeYieldAgreement
evaluated.expression: MIN(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm is only genuinely cheap if both the accrual-based and the cash-based measures of distributable profit agree; taking the lower of reported earnings yield and depreciation-charged cash-flow yield prices the firm on whichever account is less flattering, so accrual-inflated earnings cannot create apparent cheapness.
evaluated.reasoning: Unlike the gated products, this keeps a continuous, well-spread yield scale that should retain the strong FMB slope and healthy Sharpe of the additive family, while the MIN operator does the value-trap filtering inside the multiple rather than through a [0,1] gate that flattens most of the cross-section. Charging depreciation against operating cash flow prevents capital-intensive firms from looking cheap merely because their cash flow ignores capital consumption, so the two yields are economically comparable before the MIN is taken.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: MeasurementTriangulatedAccrualGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(MAX(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dpc), oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Each accrual measurement trail is individually noisy — balance-sheet differences absorb acquisitions and write-offs, cash-flow-statement accruals absorb classification choices — so a cheap firm is only credibly clean when *both* trails agree, and taking the worse (higher) of the two accrual estimates identifies genuine accrual reliance rather than measurement artifacts.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive already shows that measurement source materially changes the result (cash-flow-statement accruals gave +4.0% alpha versus +2.5% for balance-sheet accruals with a much weaker FMB slope), which means part of each leg's variation is measurement noise rather than economics; a MAX over the two trails is a triangulation operator that keeps only firms clean on both books in the long leg. This is neither the published Sloan/Hribar–Collins form nor a union with an archived expression, and by removing false-clean firms it should raise the cross-sectional slope that the single-trail gated signals lacked.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AccrualReversalCompletionGatedValue
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), INDICATOR(LAG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), 0)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: For a cheap firm the decisive question is where it stands in the accrual cycle: a firm that built up working capital last year and is now converting it into cash has already taken its earnings hit and is at the trough, whereas a firm that keeps accumulating after a prior build-up is on an escalating path of unsold inventory and uncollected receivables and its cheapness is a warning.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the cash-holdings idea with two-period accrual dynamics adds genuinely new content: the INDICATOR restricts attention to firms with a prior-year build-up, so the signed leg measures whether that specific excess is reversing or compounding, a stage-of-cycle concept absent from every archive entry (all of which use a level, average, count, volatility, or single change). Firms with no prior build-up receive zero and stay neutral, which sharpens the long and short legs onto the population where accrual reversal actually has predictive content.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EVYieldGatedCashFlowAccrual
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dpc), oancf), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among firms whose operating profit is cheap relative to total enterprise value, the firms whose profit is confirmed by operating cash flow are genuine bargains and those whose profit exists only on the accrual books are traps.
evaluated.reasoning: This crosses the archive's best gate (EBITDA/EV: the only valuation leg that preserved raw spread return, Sharpe 0.289) with its best-measured accrual leg (cash-flow-statement accruals, which produced the largest reliable alpha at +4.0%), so if the two effects are complementary rather than redundant this should dominate both parents. The main risk is coverage near 0.09 from oancf availability, which I will weigh against the balance-sheet-gated benchmark rather than against full-sample signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EVYieldGatedReversalCompletion
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), INDICATOR(LAG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), 0)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What separates a cheap firm at the earnings trough from one still deteriorating is the stage of its accrual cycle: after a prior working-capital build-up, current release means the reversal has been taken and cash is arriving, while continued accumulation means the problem is compounding.
evaluated.reasoning: Reversal-completion was the accrual leg with the strongest cross-sectional slope in the archive (FMB 2.75) while the enterprise gate was the valuation leg with the best portfolio behaviour, so this pairing directly targets the FMB-versus-alpha tension that has characterized every generation. Because the indicator restricts the signed content to firms with a prior build-up, the sort concentrates where accrual reversal has genuine predictive content instead of ranking noise.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DividendYieldGatedAccrualQuality
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Dividend yield is the one valuation multiple whose numerator is cash that has already left the firm, so it cannot be inflated by accruals; among high-yield firms, accrual quality separates payouts funded by real cash generation from payouts being sustained while receivables and inventory swell.
evaluated.reasoning: All gates tested so far use accrual-contaminated numerators (book equity, reported earnings, EBITDA), which makes the gate itself partly endogenous to the accounting quality being measured; a cash-distribution gate breaks that circularity and is also less collinear with HML than book-to-market. The sustainability-of-payout mechanism is economically distinct from anything in the archive and coverage should be good since dvc is reported as zero rather than missing for non-payers.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EVYieldGatedStockFlowDoubleHurdle
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at))), 1))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Accounting quality has both a flow and a stock dimension — this year's receivable and inventory build-up, and the accumulated bloat already sitting on the balance sheet — and a cheap firm is only trustworthy when it is clean on both, since a lean balance sheet can hide a bad year and a good year can sit atop years of accumulated softness.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive left stock versus flow unresolved: peer-relative bloat produced alpha +3.4% (t=3.4) but essentially no cross-sectional slope, while the asset-side flow produced a slope (2.6) but little alpha, which is exactly the pattern expected if each captures a different part of the truth. Taking the MIN of two separately standardized z-scores imposes a genuine double hurdle on comparable scales, so the long leg requires both conditions and the two components' complementary strengths can combine rather than average out.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SalesToEnterpriseGatedAccrualQuality
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Firms that are cheap relative to the revenue their capital supports are typically firms with temporarily depressed margins, and it is exactly in that population that accrual quality decides the outcome: a depressed-margin firm converting revenue into cash is a recovery candidate, while one whose thin profits rest on swelling receivables and inventory is a decaying business.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than tweaking the denominator of the archive's EBITDA/EV gate, this changes the gate's economic content from "cheap profit" to "cheap revenue," which selects a different and more margin-distressed population where the accrual mechanism should bite hardest, while keeping the capital-structure-neutral scaling that gave the enterprise gate its healthy raw spread. Revenue is also the least accounting-discretionary numerator available, so the gate is close to orthogonal to the accrual leg being tested, reducing the endogeneity that afflicts book-equity and earnings gates.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: LeveredIncomeIncreasingAccrualTrap
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Leverage does not make good accounting better, it makes bad accounting dangerous: only income-increasing accruals create a future reversal that must be absorbed while debt service continues, so among cheap firms the penalty for accrual-dependent earnings should scale with debt intensity and be switched off entirely for firms reporting conservative, income-decreasing accruals.
evaluated.reasoning: The asymmetry the critic identified is now explicit in the expression: INDICATOR keeps only the positive part of accruals, so firms with income-decreasing accruals receive a penalty of exactly zero regardless of leverage and no highly levered firm can be pushed into the long leg by its debt alone, which also removes the leverage main effect from the long side. Using the cross-sectional rank of debt intensity rather than its raw level prevents a handful of extremely levered firms from dominating the standardized leg while preserving the ordering that the amplification hypothesis requires.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedIncomeIncreasingAccrualOnly
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only income-increasing accruals create an obligation to reverse; income-decreasing accruals are conservatism and should earn no reward, so among firms cheap on revenue the short leg should be built purely from those inflating current earnings while the long leg holds all firms with no accrual inflation.
evaluated.reasoning: The levered asymmetric penalty produced the strongest cross-sectional slope in the entire archive (FMB 3.37) but a negative alpha, which localizes the problem in the leverage multiplier's low-leverage factor tilt rather than in the asymmetry; removing leverage and keeping the positive-part restriction should retain the slope while restoring the enterprise gate's alpha. It also directly tests whether the accrual side of the value-trap story is one-sided, a question the symmetric legs cannot answer.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorkingCapitalChargedEnterpriseYield
evaluated.expression: RATIO(SUB(ebitda, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))
evaluated.hypothesis: The correct enterprise multiple charges operating profit for the working capital the business had to absorb to produce it, so a firm is cheap only if the profit remaining after that charge is large relative to total enterprise value.
evaluated.reasoning: Every enterprise-gated signal in the archive uses a [0,1] rank gate that flattens most of the cross-section and has repeatedly produced FMB t-stats of 0.3–2.6, whereas the archive's continuous-scale signals reliably delivered FMB t-stats above 3 but only ever used equity-market deflators, which are HML-collinear. This construction is continuous *and* enterprise-scaled, embedding the accrual correction in the numerator, so it is the natural test of whether the FMB weakness of the winning family is caused by the gate's functional form rather than its economics.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: EnterpriseYieldGatedDepreciationAdequacy
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(dp, at))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The EBITDA multiple's specific blind spot is that it ignores capital consumption, so for firms that look cheap on EBITDA the decisive accounting question is depreciation adequacy: a peer-abnormally high depreciation charge means the profit being capitalized will never reach shareholders, making the apparent cheapness an artifact of the multiple's construction.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not a normalization swap but a new claim about *which* accrual matters for *which* multiple: depreciation is the largest non-cash charge and is precisely the item the enterprise gate excludes, so pairing them tests a mechanism no archived signal addresses. Note the sign is deliberately the opposite of the archived DepreciationConservatismValue, where high depreciation was rewarded because net income was already charged for it — the reversal is forced by the gate's construction, which makes the two results jointly interpretable rather than redundant.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedCollectionEfficiencyDecay
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), 5)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year's accrual build-up is mostly cyclical noise, but a multi-year upward drift in receivables-and-inventory per dollar of revenue is evidence of structural decay — lengthening collection periods and slower inventory turns — and a firm cheap on revenue with decaying collection efficiency is a business in decline rather than a mispriced asset.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive has tested accrual levels, one-year changes, three-year means, five-year volatility, five-year own-history rank and distance-from-peak, but never a fitted multi-year *slope*, which is the only statistic that distinguishes persistent directional deterioration from mean-reverting fluctuation. The economic claim is new and specific to the revenue-multiple gate: cheapness on revenue is only a bargain if that revenue is still being converted to cash at a stable or improving rate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedAccrualWithoutCashBuffer
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, at))))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: An accrual reversal is an accounting event for a cash-rich firm but a financing event for a cash-poor one, because the unwind of receivables and inventory has to be funded; the value trap is therefore the joint state of cheap price, income-increasing accruals, and no liquidity buffer to absorb the reversal.
evaluated.reasoning: This adds a genuinely new conditioning dimension — the balance-sheet liquidity cushion — rather than another deflator, and it is deliberately built to avoid the failure of the earlier leverage-weighted version: the INDICATOR restricts amplification to income-increasing accruals, so a cash-poor firm with conservative accruals receives exactly zero penalty and cannot enter the long leg on liquidity grounds alone. Using the cross-sectional rank of cash scarcity keeps the weight bounded in [0,1] so a few cash-hoarding firms cannot dominate the standardized leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedUnjustifiedWorkingCapitalInvestment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), MUL(GROWTH(sale, 1), LAG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at), 1)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Working capital should grow in proportion to revenue, so the benchmark for normal accrual investment is last year's working-capital intensity scaled by this year's revenue growth; only the excess over that benchmark represents receivables and inventory accumulating without corresponding business expansion, which is the accounting signature of a value trap.
evaluated.reasoning: This implements an explicit expectation model for normal accruals — the symbolic analogue of the Jones-model fitted value — instead of the crude industry demeaning that made the earlier discretionary-accrual attempt fail (alpha 0.2%, t 0.14), and it is continuous with no degenerate mass point. It also sharpens the interaction with the revenue-multiple gate: a firm cheap on revenue that is investing in working capital faster than its revenue justifies is exactly the case where cheapness reflects deteriorating fundamentals rather than mispricing.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedPureWorkingCapitalAccrual
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), at)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The value-trap mechanism is about working capital — receivables and inventory accumulating without cash — and depreciation belongs to capital intensity rather than earnings manipulation, so removing the depreciation term should leave the economically relevant accrual signal intact.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the exact complement of Signal 1: together they partition the champion's leg into its depreciation and working-capital components under an unchanged gate, so whichever carries the +4.4% alpha and the 2.48 slope is identified rather than inferred. The distinction matters economically because a depreciation-driven result is a capital-intensity/conservatism story while a working-capital-driven result is the accrual-quality story this project is about.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedWorkingCapitalRelease
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 0))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The abnormal return in cheap stocks comes from firms actively liquidating working capital into cash — collections improving, inventories clearing — a self-help operational turn the market underprices, whereas the absence of accrual inflation by itself is not rewarded.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the mirror image of the positive-part tests whose slopes were the archive's strongest but whose alphas were negative, which logically locates the champion's abnormal return in the negative-accrual tail; scoring only the magnitude of working-capital *releases* tests that inference directly. If it delivers alpha comparable to the champion with a positive slope, the economic story sharpens from "avoid accrual-inflated cheap firms" to "buy cheap firms converting working capital into cash."
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashCollectedRevenueToEnterprise
evaluated.expression: RATIO(SUB(sale, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))
evaluated.hypothesis: The right revenue multiple charges revenue for the portion that was not collected but instead parked in receivables and inventory, so cash-collected revenue per dollar of enterprise value is the accrual-proof version of the sales multiple.
evaluated.reasoning: The continuous-form test so far charged *EBITDA* for working capital, which turned it into a cash-flow yield that FF5 spans (alpha −1.9% despite FMB 3.11); applying the same correction to the revenue line instead keeps the signal a top-line multiple, which is a different factor exposure profile and matches the gate that has worked best. It also preserves a continuous, well-spread scale, addressing the persistent FMB weakness of the rank-gated family without reverting to a profit-based cash-flow yield.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedCashShareConversion
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(che, act), 1), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Collection is directly observable as a shift in the composition of current assets: when cash rises as a share of current assets, receivables and inventory are being converted into money, and a cheap firm showing that shift is realizing the value its balance sheet claims rather than accumulating paper claims.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the depreciation channel entirely, along with its sign-fitting problem, and replaces it with a conversion-event mechanism: taking the *change* in the cash share removes the static industry and size differences that made the level version of che/act uninformative, leaving only the year-over-year liquidity transformation. It is also a scale-free composition measure requiring no deflator choice, so it is not a variant of any asset-scaled accrual leg in the archive, and coverage should be high since only act and che are needed over two years.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedOwnScaleAccrualSurprise
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), MA(ABS(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A given accrual is only informative relative to how large that firm's accruals normally are: a distributor whose working capital routinely swings by five percent of assets is not manipulating earnings when it does so again, while the same swing at a firm that normally reports negligible accruals is a genuine anomaly.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than averaging two correlated horizons, this uses the firm's own three-year mean absolute accrual as the *scaling* denominator, converting the cross-sectional accrual level into a firm-specific standardized surprise — the only construction in the archive where the accrual is normalized by its own dispersion rather than by a balance-sheet or income deflator. The denominator is an absolute value so it cannot invert the sign, and the mechanism is economically distinct from the earlier difference-from-mean surprise because it identifies unusual accrual *magnitude relative to habitual volatility*, which is what separates opportunistic reporting from ordinary business-model variation.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: RevenueGatedAccrualPerUnitOperatingProfit
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful measure of accrual reliance is how much working-capital investment the firm absorbed per dollar of the operating profit it habitually earns; when a year's working-capital build-up rivals the firm's normal profit, the reported earnings have no cash counterpart.
evaluated.reasoning: The sign-inversion defect is repaired exactly where the critic located it: the deflator is now the three-year mean of absolute operating profit, which is strictly positive so loss-making firms can no longer be scored as clean, and the smoothing prevents a single near-zero EBITDA year from exploding the ratio. Deflating by earnings power rather than by assets or sales is the one scaling the archive has never tested with a stable denominator, and it is the most literal statement of the project's premise that earnings quality is about the cash backing of profit.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NormalizedEarningsPowerGateAccrual
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(ebitda, 3), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness should be judged against normalized rather than spot profitability, because a single depressed or inflated EBITDA year misclassifies cyclical firms; a firm trading cheaply relative to its three-year average operating profit is genuinely cheap, and that is the population where accrual quality decides the outcome.
evaluated.reasoning: Both the current champion and its predecessor use spot multiples in the gate while the winning accrual leg uses smoothed earnings power, an internal inconsistency worth resolving: normalizing the gate the same way makes the conditioning variable measure durable cheapness rather than a one-year earnings dip. This is a change to the economic definition of the gate rather than a denominator tweak, and if it lifts both the slope and the alpha it tells us the champion has been partly conditioning on cyclical noise.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AssetSideAccrualPerEarningsPower
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The trap mechanism is revenue booked but not collected and goods produced but not sold, so the asset side of working capital alone should carry the signal, while operating liabilities reflect supplier financing that is not an earnings-quality problem.
evaluated.reasoning: Under an asset deflator and a book-to-market gate, the asset-side-only leg earned little alpha (1.0%, t 1.06) while the netted version earned 2.5%, but that test predates both the revenue gate and the earnings-power deflator, so the decomposition needs to be redone in the winning configuration before the final round. It also tests directly whether the liability side belongs in the measure — the question the gross-churn inversion first raised and no configuration has resolved cleanly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitDestinationCashVersusWorkingCapital
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dvc, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Profit has to go somewhere, and where it goes reveals whether it was real: a cheap firm that sends earnings to shareholders as cash dividends has demonstrably converted profit into money, whereas one whose earnings disappear into growing receivables and inventory has not, so the net flow of profit toward owners versus toward working capital is the sharpest earnings-quality test available.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a new mechanism rather than another deflator: it places a hard cash outflow (dividends) and a soft accrual absorption on the same earnings-power scale and takes their difference, so it measures the *destination* of profit instead of only its accrual content. Because dividends and working-capital investment are largely independent decisions, the combined leg should carry information beyond the champion's accrual-only measure, and the dividend-gated test already showed the payout channel is informative (alpha 3.4%, t 3.20) without contaminating the gate.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: SupplierCreditPerEarningsPower
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Growth in operating liabilities is not an earnings-quality defect but interest-free financing extended by suppliers and employees to firms they expect to survive, so among cheap firms an expanding operating-liability base relative to earnings power signals bargaining power and funding relief rather than accrual inflation.
evaluated.reasoning: This completes the decomposition begun by the accepted asset-side test: the two proposals together partition the champion's netted accrual leg under the winning gate and deflator, and the sign here is deliberately *unnegated*, which makes it a falsifiable economic claim rather than a smoothing tweak. The archive already produced indirect evidence for it — penalizing operating-liability growth with the same sign as asset growth inverted the alpha from +2.5% to −2.3% — but the liability side has never been tested on its own, so this establishes whether Sloan's netting is genuinely required or whether the asset side is doing all the work.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorkingCapitalStockPerEarningsPower
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: A business that must keep several years' worth of operating profit permanently locked in receivables and inventory has a structurally poor claim on its own book value, because that capital is illiquid and impairable; a cheap firm with a light working-capital stock relative to its earnings power owns assets it can actually monetize.
evaluated.reasoning: This is the *level*, not any difference, so it cannot telescope into the flow measure the critic identified, and it resolves the stock-versus-flow question in the winning configuration: the bloat level previously earned alpha of +3.4% but no cross-sectional slope under an asset deflator and a book-to-market gate, and the untested question is whether the earnings-power deflator supplies the missing slope by turning capital intensity into an interpretable "years of profit tied up" quantity. Because it needs no differencing, coverage should be at or above the champion's 0.110.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: DebtFundedWorkingCapitalAbsorption
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The dangerous configuration is not accrual absorption alone but accrual absorption financed by short-term borrowing: when a cheap firm's profit disappears into receivables and inventory while its current debt simultaneously expands relative to earnings power, the working-capital cycle is being funded by lenders who can withdraw, which is the standard pre-distress sequence.
evaluated.reasoning: This asks a new economic question — the *funding source* of the accrual, measured as a flow of short-term credit — rather than reweighting tails of an existing leg to chase in-sample statistics, and it differs from the earlier cash-buffer and total-leverage tests, which used stock-based scarcity or debt-intensity multipliers rather than the contemporaneous change in current debt. Both components are placed on the same earnings-power scale so their sum is interpretable as "profit absorbed plus short-term credit drawn, per dollar of normal profit," and the leg stays continuous with no censoring or point mass.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AssetBuildupAndShortTermDebtDraw
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The trap configuration is uncollected revenue and unsold inventory financed by short-term borrowing; growth in other operating liabilities should get no credit at all, because supplier and accrued liabilities are as much a symptom of strain as a source of free financing.
evaluated.reasoning: The winning leg algebraically credits total current-liability growth while double-penalizing current debt, and the standalone liability test produced a wrong-signed slope (FMB −2.445), so the coherent version penalizes asset-side absorption and debt draw and credits neither. This isolates whether the champion's strength survives removal of the liability-reward term, which is the last unresolved sign question in the leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: TotalDebtFundedWorkingCapitalAbsorption
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters is that the working-capital cycle is being financed by creditors rather than by operations, and long-term borrowing funds the same absorption as short-term borrowing while merely postponing the refinancing date.
evaluated.reasoning: The short-term-debt version delivered the archive's best joint result, so the immediate question is whether the mechanism is about rollover risk specifically or about creditor funding of accruals generally; using total debt issuance answers it in one test. If total debt performs as well, the economic story broadens from a liquidity-timing story to an external-financing story, and if it performs worse the maturity structure is essential.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: WorkingCapitalAbsorptionWithRolloverExposure
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(dlc, MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The danger is the standing stock of debt that must be refinanced within a year measured against normal profit, not merely this year's incremental draw: a cheap firm absorbing profit into working capital while carrying several years of earnings power in current debt has no margin for the reversal.
evaluated.reasoning: Substituting the level of current debt for its change tests state versus flow in the funding dimension, the same distinction that mattered on the accrual side, and levels are far more persistent than annual changes, so if the state version holds up it should lower turnover and stabilize portfolio composition further. It also guards against the possibility that the champion's Δdlc term is picking up transitory financing noise rather than genuine rollover exposure.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: NormalizedGateDebtFundedAbsorption
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(ebitda, 3), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Cheapness should be judged against normalized earnings power rather than a single year's revenue, so the firms in which the funding-augmented accrual test bites hardest are those trading cheaply relative to the profit they can sustain through a cycle.
evaluated.reasoning: The two best-performing design choices of generation 8 were the funding-augmented leg (Sharpe 0.553) and the smoothed earnings-power gate (alpha 4.1%, t 3.84), and they have never been combined; since the leg's deflator is already three-year mean profit, this also makes the gate and leg internally consistent in what they treat as earnings power. It is a deliberate final-round consolidation, and its value is that it either confirms the revenue gate is doing something the profit gate cannot, or delivers the strongest configuration in the archive.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: ProfitUsesIdentityPerEarningsPower
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(dvc, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), DELTA(dlc, 1)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Earnings quality is fully described by where the profit went: cash paid to owners is proof of conversion, profit absorbed into receivables and inventory is unproven, and short-term credit drawn is proof that the profit never arrived — the net of these three, scaled by normal profit, is the complete test of whether a cheap firm's earnings are real.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a single accounting identity rather than a weighted blend of standardized legs: the dividend and absorption terms already earned +3.1% (t 3.34) and the absorption-plus-debt terms +3.8% (t 4.30), and they describe complementary uses of the same profit, so combining them within one ratio imposes economic rather than statistical weights. It is the most complete statement of the project's premise — that value is trustworthy only when reported profit shows up as cash — and it is the natural signal to carry forward if it holds both the slope and the alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: AbsorptionVersusFundsFromOperations
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), ADD(ib, dp)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The economically meaningful funding test is whether the working capital a firm absorbed this year was covered by the funds its operations actually generated — net income plus the depreciation add-back — because when absorption exceeds funds from operations the firm must go to creditors or shareholders, and a cheap firm in that position is a trap regardless of what its income statement says.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces Δche, which as noted is a residual of operating, investing and financing flows and duplicates the cash term already netted inside working capital, with funds from operations (ib + dp), the standard internal-funding measure and one that is broadly populated so coverage stays near 0.110 rather than dropping to cash-flow-statement levels. It is the internal-funding complement to the archive's winning external-funding term: that signal asks whether creditors financed the accrual, this asks whether operations could have, and both are expressed per unit of normal earnings power so the magnitudes are interpretable.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: EVCashYieldMinusWCBuildup
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che)), NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(wcap, che), 1), at)))
considered.hypothesis: A low enterprise multiple is attractive only if the operating profit behind it is not being generated by inflating non-cash working capital; balance-sheet accrual buildup signals that EBITDA overstates distributable cash.
considered.reasoning: Using EV (equity plus debt minus cash) makes the valuation leg capital-structure neutral and directly comparable to EBITDA, while the change in non-cash working capital (wcap net of cash) is the balance-sheet measure of accruals that pollutes EBITDA. Combining a high EBITDA/EV rank with a low working-capital-accrual rank targets firms that are cheap on cash-generating operations rather than on accounting-inflated operating income.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueWithStableAccruals
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Investors mistrust cheap firms whose accrual behavior is erratic; unstable accruals indicate opaque, hard-to-value accounting, so the value discount of firms with smooth, predictable accruals is more likely to be a genuine mispricing that corrects.
considered.reasoning: Rather than the level of accruals, this uses the five-year volatility of the accrual ratio as an accounting-opacity proxy, capturing a second-moment earnings-quality mechanism distinct from high-versus-low accrual sorts. Cheap firms with stable accruals should earn the value premium, whereas cheap firms with volatile accruals are information-risk value traps whose book values are unreliable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashVerifiedBookToMarket
considered.expression: RATIO(SUB(ceq, TS_SUM(SUB(ib, oancf), 5)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))
considered.hypothesis: Reported book equity is the accumulation of past earnings, part of which was never collected in cash; stripping five years of cumulative accruals from book equity yields a cash-verified book value, and the discount of price to that hardened book value is the true value signal.
considered.reasoning: Instead of stacking two known anomalies additively, this restates the valuation numerator itself: cumulative accruals (TS_SUM of ib - oancf) measure how much of retained equity is soft accounting rather than realized cash, so subtracting them re-prices the firm on cash-verified net worth. A cheap firm whose book equity is largely accrual accumulation loses its apparent discount, which is exactly the value-trap mechanism, while genuinely cheap cash-generating firms keep or increase their score.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYieldEarningsYieldRankGap
considered.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: The market prices the earnings-based multiple, so firms that look only moderately cheap on earnings but very cheap on operating cash flow are systematically underpriced, while firms that look cheap on earnings only because accruals inflate those earnings are overpriced.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are valuation multiples on the same price denominator, so their rank gap isolates the wedge between cash-based and accrual-based cheapness rather than pooling a value score with an accrual score. Unlike a MIN operator, the difference preserves full ordering in both tails: the short leg is populated by firms whose earnings yield rank far exceeds their cash yield rank (accrual-supported cheapness) and the long leg by cash-rich firms whose reported earnings understate cash generation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualQualityAmplifiedByCheapness
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ib, oancf), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Earnings-quality information is priced least efficiently among value stocks, where investors already expect weak fundamentals, so the accrual signal should be amplified by cheapness and switched off among glamour stocks.
considered.reasoning: The cheapness leg enters as a bounded rank weight in (0,1), which removes the negative-book-equity pathology of using raw book-to-market as a multiplier (negative-equity firms sit at rank ~0 and are neutralized rather than sign-flipped), while the winsorized accrual z-score carries the signed direction of the signal. The construction is deliberately asymmetric: it goes long cheap-and-cash-backed firms, short cheap-and-accrual-inflated firms, and takes near-zero positions in expensive names, which is a conditional amplification rather than an additive stack.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SalesYieldNonCashCurrentAssetDrag
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale)))
considered.hypothesis: A low price-to-sales multiple is a bargain only when revenue is collected rather than parked in receivables and inventory; firms whose non-cash current assets balloon relative to sales are recognizing revenue that has not converted to cash.
considered.reasoning: The revenue-quality leg is now built from balance-sheet items with broad coverage (act, che, sale) instead of the sparse and sign-inconsistent cash-flow-statement components, and it excludes payables entirely so that stretching suppliers can no longer masquerade as high quality. Scaling the change in non-cash current assets by sales makes the two legs conceptually matched: both are per-dollar-of-revenue measures, so the composite isolates cheap firms whose revenue base is genuinely cash-converting.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Accounting quality is priced least efficiently inside the value tail; among cheap firms, low balance-sheet accruals identify genuine bargains and high accruals identify value traps, while among glamour firms the accrual signal carries little incremental information.
considered.reasoning: The bounded cheapness rank acts as a conditioning weight (near zero for expensive and negative-book-equity firms, so no sign pathology), and the signed, winsorized balance-sheet accrual z-score supplies direction, so the long-short spread is long cheap-and-clean versus short cheap-and-dirty. Because both legs sit in the value/low-price region, HML and CMA loadings largely cancel, which is exactly the structural fix for the near-zero FF5 alphas of generation 0's additive composites.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueWithStableWorkingCapital
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(VOL(RATIO(wcap, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Erratic working capital signals opaque, hard-to-audit accounting, so investors rationally discount such firms; cheap firms with smooth working-capital intensity are more likely to be genuine mispricings whose value discount closes.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the invalidated second-moment idea using an accrual-exclusive state variable (wcap) whose five-year volatility is computable from annual balance sheets with wide coverage. It tests an information-risk mechanism rather than an accrual-level mechanism, so if the level-based composites keep getting absorbed by FF5, a dispersion-based accounting-opacity leg tells us something new about which cheap firms are traps.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueWithNOWCAtOwnHistoryLow
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: Working-capital norms differ enormously across business models, so what matters is whether a firm's non-cash working capital sits high or low relative to its own five-year history; cheap firms whose balance sheet is currently lean by their own standard have already worked off past accruals and face no reversal drag.
considered.reasoning: This drops the discredited "linear-in-B/M" construction and replaces the cross-sectional accrual level with a within-firm time-series position (TS_RANK), which removes industry and business-model differences in normal working-capital intensity that contaminate cross-sectional accrual ranks. It is therefore mechanistically distinct from the archive's cross-sectional level, flow, and volatility legs, and it avoids negative-numerator distress artifacts because the valuation leg keeps standard book equity.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DepreciationConservatismValue
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ni, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(dp, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Depreciation is the largest non-discretionary negative accrual; firms that depreciate aggressively relative to industry peers understate reported earnings, so a high earnings yield achieved despite conservative accounting understates true cash profitability and is systematically underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This is the mirror image of the usual accrual story and is not a reconstruction of cash-flow-to-price: the signal deliberately rewards a *large* negative accrual, so it separates firms that are cheap because earnings are conservatively stated from firms that are cheap on inflated income. Industry z-scoring of dp/at is essential because depreciation intensity mostly reflects capital intensity, and it makes the accounting-conservatism component orthogonal to sector composition.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EarningsYieldAsymmetricAccrualPenalty
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(ni, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(MUL(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), INDICATOR(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), 0))))
considered.hypothesis: Only income-increasing accruals carry manipulation content; working-capital releases (negative accruals) reflect operating discipline or conservatism rather than inflated earnings, so the value signal should be penalized for accrual build-ups but not symmetrically rewarded for run-downs.
considered.reasoning: The tax-payable leg is abandoned because, as noted, Δtxp is itself a current-liability accrual and too small and sparse to carry half the signal weight; it is replaced by a positive-part accrual penalty built with INDICATOR, which imposes an economically motivated asymmetry rather than a linear accrual rank. This isolates a specific design question the archive cannot answer: whether the value-trap effect is driven entirely by the income-increasing tail of accruals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SalesYieldReceivableGrowthDivergence
considered.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), NEG(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(act, che), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Revenue quality is revealed by whether non-cash current assets grow faster than the revenue they support; a low price-to-sales multiple is a genuine bargain only when receivables and inventory are not outrunning sales.
considered.reasoning: This fixes the cash-contamination flaw by explicitly excluding che from the working-capital measure, so cash accumulation no longer looks like accrual bloat, and it changes the statistic rather than the horizon: a growth-rate divergence is scale-free and directly matched to the sales-based valuation leg, unlike an asset-scaled level change. The receivables-versus-sales growth gap is the classic revenue-recognition red flag, giving a clean test of whether cheap-on-sales firms with deteriorating revenue quality are the traps.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValuePremiumGatedByCleanAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The value premium exists only where reported fundamentals are trustworthy: among clean-accrual firms cheapness predicts high returns, while among accrual-inflated firms book value is unreliable and the value spread should be flat or perverse.
considered.reasoning: This inverts the conditioning of the archive's only alpha-positive signal — accrual quality becomes the bounded gate and signed cheapness carries direction — so the long-short spread is long cheap-clean versus short expensive-clean, holding accounting quality high in both legs. Comparing its alpha to ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual identifies whether the interaction is a value effect concentrated in clean firms or an accrual effect concentrated in cheap firms, which is the single most informative unresolved design question in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PercentAccrualGatedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), ABS(ib))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What matters for a high earnings yield is the share of that income which is accrual rather than cash, so accruals should be deflated by the magnitude of earnings, not by assets; a cheap-on-earnings firm whose income is mostly accrual is a trap regardless of its asset base.
considered.reasoning: Scaling accruals by absolute earnings makes the accrual leg commensurate with the earnings-yield valuation leg, so the interaction measures the reliability of the very quantity being capitalized, unlike asset-scaled accruals which mix in capital intensity. This isolates the deflator design choice against the gen-1 winner while switching the valuation channel from book-to-market to earnings yield, giving a cleaner economic reading of "cheap on earnings that are actually cash."
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueWithGrossOperatingBalanceSheetChurn
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), sale), RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1), sale))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Sloan accruals net asset-side buildup against liability-side buildup, but for a cheap firm both are bad news: growing receivables and inventory signal unsold or uncollected revenue, while growing payables and accrued liabilities signal stretched suppliers and funding strain, so the two should enter with the same sign rather than opposite signs.
considered.reasoning: This is a decomposition test of the accrual leg itself: if the netted Sloan measure works only because of its asset side, then a gross-churn version that also penalizes operating-liability expansion should perform at least as well among value stocks and better in the distress tail. Sales scaling keeps both components commensurate with operating volume and avoids the capital-intensity contamination of asset scaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueWithPersistentlyCleanAccruals
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 0), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: A single year of low accruals can be luck or a one-off working-capital release; a multi-year record of income-decreasing accruals reveals a conservative reporting policy, and cheap firms with such a record are the ones whose book value can be trusted.
considered.reasoning: This repairs the failure of ValueWithStableWorkingCapital, whose FF5 alpha was significantly negative (−3.4%/yr, t = −3.5) partly because VOL over five annual points is a very noisy second moment and raw wcap measures cash-holding variability rather than accounting policy. Counting the number of clean-accrual years is a robust persistence statistic on a properly cash-excluded accrual measure, testing whether reporting-policy consistency, rather than accrual dispersion, is what distinguishes real value from value traps.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ValueWithWorkingCapitalOffItsPeak
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(TS_MAX(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 5), RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale)), 1)))
