considered.hypothesis: Accrual bloat is a state, not a flow: a cheap firm whose non-cash working-capital intensity now sits far below its own five-year peak has already absorbed and reversed its accrual excess, so its depressed earnings are the trough rather than the start of a decline, whereas a cheap firm sitting at its own peak still has the reversal ahead of it.
considered.reasoning: The telescoping and 1/price problems are both removed: distance-from-own-peak is a genuine level state that cannot collapse into a five-year difference, and no fundamental is divided by market cap, so the signal is not a repackaged accrual-to-price ratio. It retains the value-gated multiplicative architecture because that is the only form in the archive that produced a reliable FF5 alpha (both legs are cheap stocks so HML and CMA cancel), while the accrual content — reversal stage measured against the firm's own history — is new relative to level, gross-churn, percent, and persistence versions already queued.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DeratingWithCleanAccrualSurprise
considered.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(SUB(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What identifies a value trap is not a low valuation level but a *de-rating* accompanied by deteriorating accounting: when a firm becomes cheap relative to its own valuation history while its accruals rise above their own multi-year norm, the price decline is confirmation of fundamental erosion; when the same de-rating occurs with accruals below their own norm, it is sentiment-driven mispricing that reverts.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are benchmarked to the firm's own history — a time-series cheapness position and an accrual surprise relative to its own three-year average — so the construction is industry- and business-model-free by design rather than by mechanical demeaning, and it adds new economic content (de-rating dynamics interacted with accrual deterioration) instead of re-scaling the gen-1 winner. The accrual leg is winsorized before z-scoring, fixing the outlier exposure the critic identified.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashFlowStatementAccrualGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dpc), oancf), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among cheap firms, the reliability of reported earnings is best measured by the wedge between income before depreciation and actual operating cash flow, because balance-sheet differences also move with acquisitions, divestitures and write-offs that have nothing to do with earnings quality.
considered.reasoning: Every accrual leg tested so far has been a balance-sheet delta; measuring working-capital accruals directly from the cash-flow statement (ib + dpc − oancf) removes non-articulation noise and should sharpen both the cross-sectional slope and the portfolio spread if measurement error was diluting the archive's gated signals. It keeps the cheapness gate that the evidence shows is required for FF5 alpha, so any change in performance is attributable to accrual measurement alone.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AssetSideAccrualGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The value-trap effect comes from the asset side of accruals — receivables and inventory that represent revenue not yet collected or sold — while operating-liability growth is a financing/liquidity phenomenon that carries the opposite return sign.
considered.reasoning: The gross-churn test showed that adding operating-liability growth with a penalizing sign flips the FF5 alpha from +2.5% to −2.3%, which implies the liability side works in the opposite direction; the clean follow-up is to strip the liability side out entirely and see whether asset-side buildup alone reproduces or beats the netted Sloan measure. If it does, the mechanism is specifically about uncollected revenue and unsold inventory rather than total accrual accounting.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicAccrualRelianceGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A single year of accruals is a noisy read on accounting quality; what makes a cheap firm a trap is chronic, multi-year reliance on accruals to report income, and the average accrual rate over three years measures that reliance while preserving magnitude.
considered.reasoning: The persistence-count repair failed (alpha −1.9%) precisely because a 0–5 count throws away how large the accruals were, so the better fix is a magnitude-preserving three-year mean, which also reduces annual re-ranking and should raise the poor Sharpe (0.20) of the gated family. If chronic accrual reliance beats the one-year measure, the mechanism is a persistent reporting-policy effect rather than a one-year reversal effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SoftBookShareGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), ceq)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Book-to-market is only trustworthy if book equity is composed of hard assets; when most of a cheap firm's equity is non-cash working capital, the denominator of its value case is soft accrual-based accounting subject to write-down, making the discount illusory.
considered.reasoning: This attacks the accrual stock embedded in the value ratio's own numerator rather than the annual accrual flow, so it tests bloat versus flow as the operative concept, and unlike the earlier "hard book-to-market" attempt it stays multiplicative-conditional and never creates negative or uninterpretable numerators. It requires no differencing or multi-year window, so coverage should exceed the archive's typical 0.105–0.11 and portfolio composition should be more stable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SalesDeflatedAccrualGatedEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), sale)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: For a firm that looks cheap on earnings, the relevant question is how much accrual accounting was needed per dollar of revenue to produce those earnings; revenue is a stable, always-positive deflator that keeps the accrual measure comparable without exploding for marginally profitable firms.
considered.reasoning: The earnings-yield-gated version produced the archive's most reliable alpha (2.9%, t=2.8) but a weak FMB t of 1.4, and the likely culprit is the ABS(ib) deflator, which explodes near zero earnings and creates extreme, non-monotone signal values exactly among the marginal firms; sales deflation preserves the "accrual intensity of reported profit" idea with a well-behaved scale. This isolates the deflator choice while keeping the earnings-yield gate whose alpha evidence is the strongest in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DiscretionaryWCAccrualGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), sale), 1))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Not all accruals are discretionary: working capital that grows in proportion to revenue is the normal cost of doing business, and industry-wide swings in receivable and inventory intensity reflect credit and demand cycles, so only the residual — a rise in working-capital-to-sales beyond the firm's revenue scale and beyond its industry's contemporaneous move — indicates earnings that were manufactured rather than earned.
considered.reasoning: Every accrual leg in the archive measures *total* accruals, so the untested economic question is whether the value-trap effect comes from the discretionary component; differencing the working-capital-to-sales ratio removes growth-justified accrual investment mechanically, and IND_ADJ then removes the common industry cycle, leaving a firm-specific abnormal accrual. This replaces the mechanical re-blend with a normal-versus-discretionary decomposition, and because the residual is a much cleaner manipulation proxy it should sharpen the cross-sectional slope while retaining the value-gated architecture that is the only one delivering FF5 alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ReceivableInventoryCashDrainGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(ADD(RATIO(recch, at), RATIO(invch, at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The value-trap channel is specifically that revenue has been booked but not collected and goods produced but not sold, and the cash-flow statement reports these two drains directly rather than inferring them from contaminated balance-sheet differences.
considered.reasoning: Two separate archive results point here: cash-flow-statement measurement produced the best alpha of any accrual leg, and the gross-churn failure showed the liability side works in the opposite direction, so the natural intersection is the asset-side components measured from the cash-flow statement. Compustat reports recch and invch as cash-flow effects (positive when receivables or inventory are released), so the leg enters unnegated, and coverage is the main risk to monitor.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PeerRelativeBloatGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Working-capital bloat only signals soft accounting when it is abnormal for the firm's line of business; distributors and manufacturers require structurally high working capital, so the trap indicator is bloat relative to industry peers, scaled by total assets rather than by fragile book equity.
considered.reasoning: The soft-book version produced a large alpha (+4.1%) but a wrong-signed FMB t and negative Sharpe, exactly what one expects if the ratio is unstable in the distressed tail (small or negative ceq) and is partly sorting on working-capital-intensive industries. Replacing the denominator with total assets and demeaning within industry fixes both defects while keeping the stock-versus-flow question that motivated it.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EVYieldGatedAccrualQuality
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Accrual quality should be evaluated conditional on how cheap the firm's operating cash-generating capacity is relative to its whole capital structure, not on book-to-market, because the enterprise multiple identifies cheapness without the leverage and write-off distortions embedded in book equity.
considered.reasoning: Every gated signal so far has used a price-to-book or price-to-earnings gate, which is nearly collinear with HML, so the resulting spread earns alpha mainly through negative factor loadings while its raw return stays near zero (Sharpe 0.03–0.19); the EBITDA/EV gate was the archive's best raw-return valuation leg (Sharpe 0.283). Swapping the gate isolates whether the gated family's weak Sharpe is a HML-collinearity problem rather than an accrual-measurement problem.

considered.name: ConservativeYieldAgreement
considered.expression: MIN(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))
considered.hypothesis: A firm is only genuinely cheap if both the accrual-based and the cash-based measures of distributable profit agree; taking the lower of reported earnings yield and depreciation-charged cash-flow yield prices the firm on whichever account is less flattering, so accrual-inflated earnings cannot create apparent cheapness.
considered.reasoning: Unlike the gated products, this keeps a continuous, well-spread yield scale that should retain the strong FMB slope and healthy Sharpe of the additive family, while the MIN operator does the value-trap filtering inside the multiple rather than through a [0,1] gate that flattens most of the cross-section. Charging depreciation against operating cash flow prevents capital-intensive firms from looking cheap merely because their cash flow ignores capital consumption, so the two yields are economically comparable before the MIN is taken.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MeasurementTriangulatedAccrualGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), NEG(ZSCORE(WINSOR(MAX(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dpc), oancf), at), RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Each accrual measurement trail is individually noisy — balance-sheet differences absorb acquisitions and write-offs, cash-flow-statement accruals absorb classification choices — so a cheap firm is only credibly clean when *both* trails agree, and taking the worse (higher) of the two accrual estimates identifies genuine accrual reliance rather than measurement artifacts.
considered.reasoning: The archive already shows that measurement source materially changes the result (cash-flow-statement accruals gave +4.0% alpha versus +2.5% for balance-sheet accruals with a much weaker FMB slope), which means part of each leg's variation is measurement noise rather than economics; a MAX over the two trails is a triangulation operator that keeps only firms clean on both books in the long leg. This is neither the published Sloan/Hribar–Collins form nor a union with an archived expression, and by removing false-clean firms it should raise the cross-sectional slope that the single-trail gated signals lacked.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccrualReversalCompletionGatedValue
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), INDICATOR(LAG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), 0)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: For a cheap firm the decisive question is where it stands in the accrual cycle: a firm that built up working capital last year and is now converting it into cash has already taken its earnings hit and is at the trough, whereas a firm that keeps accumulating after a prior build-up is on an escalating path of unsold inventory and uncollected receivables and its cheapness is a warning.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the cash-holdings idea with two-period accrual dynamics adds genuinely new content: the INDICATOR restricts attention to firms with a prior-year build-up, so the signed leg measures whether that specific excess is reversing or compounding, a stage-of-cycle concept absent from every archive entry (all of which use a level, average, count, volatility, or single change). Firms with no prior build-up receive zero and stay neutral, which sharpens the long and short legs onto the population where accrual reversal actually has predictive content.

considered.name: EVYieldGatedCashFlowAccrual
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dpc), oancf), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Among firms whose operating profit is cheap relative to total enterprise value, the firms whose profit is confirmed by operating cash flow are genuine bargains and those whose profit exists only on the accrual books are traps.
considered.reasoning: This crosses the archive's best gate (EBITDA/EV: the only valuation leg that preserved raw spread return, Sharpe 0.289) with its best-measured accrual leg (cash-flow-statement accruals, which produced the largest reliable alpha at +4.0%), so if the two effects are complementary rather than redundant this should dominate both parents. The main risk is coverage near 0.09 from oancf availability, which I will weigh against the balance-sheet-gated benchmark rather than against full-sample signals.

considered.name: EVYieldGatedReversalCompletion
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(MUL(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at)), INDICATOR(LAG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), 1), 0)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What separates a cheap firm at the earnings trough from one still deteriorating is the stage of its accrual cycle: after a prior working-capital build-up, current release means the reversal has been taken and cash is arriving, while continued accumulation means the problem is compounding.
considered.reasoning: Reversal-completion was the accrual leg with the strongest cross-sectional slope in the archive (FMB 2.75) while the enterprise gate was the valuation leg with the best portfolio behaviour, so this pairing directly targets the FMB-versus-alpha tension that has characterized every generation. Because the indicator restricts the signed content to firms with a prior build-up, the sort concentrates where accrual reversal has genuine predictive content instead of ranking noise.

considered.name: DividendYieldGatedAccrualQuality
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(dvc, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Dividend yield is the one valuation multiple whose numerator is cash that has already left the firm, so it cannot be inflated by accruals; among high-yield firms, accrual quality separates payouts funded by real cash generation from payouts being sustained while receivables and inventory swell.
considered.reasoning: All gates tested so far use accrual-contaminated numerators (book equity, reported earnings, EBITDA), which makes the gate itself partly endogenous to the accounting quality being measured; a cash-distribution gate breaks that circularity and is also less collinear with HML than book-to-market. The sustainability-of-payout mechanism is economically distinct from anything in the archive and coverage should be good since dvc is reported as zero rather than missing for non-payers.

considered.name: EVYieldGatedStockFlowDoubleHurdle
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), MIN(ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), at)), 1)), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at))), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Accounting quality has both a flow and a stock dimension — this year's receivable and inventory build-up, and the accumulated bloat already sitting on the balance sheet — and a cheap firm is only trustworthy when it is clean on both, since a lean balance sheet can hide a bad year and a good year can sit atop years of accumulated softness.
considered.reasoning: The archive left stock versus flow unresolved: peer-relative bloat produced alpha +3.4% (t=3.4) but essentially no cross-sectional slope, while the asset-side flow produced a slope (2.6) but little alpha, which is exactly the pattern expected if each captures a different part of the truth. Taking the MIN of two separately standardized z-scores imposes a genuine double hurdle on comparable scales, so the long leg requires both conditions and the two components' complementary strengths can combine rather than average out.

considered.name: SalesToEnterpriseGatedAccrualQuality
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that are cheap relative to the revenue their capital supports are typically firms with temporarily depressed margins, and it is exactly in that population that accrual quality decides the outcome: a depressed-margin firm converting revenue into cash is a recovery candidate, while one whose thin profits rest on swelling receivables and inventory is a decaying business.
considered.reasoning: Rather than tweaking the denominator of the archive's EBITDA/EV gate, this changes the gate's economic content from "cheap profit" to "cheap revenue," which selects a different and more margin-distressed population where the accrual mechanism should bite hardest, while keeping the capital-structure-neutral scaling that gave the enterprise gate its healthy raw spread. Revenue is also the least accounting-discretionary numerator available, so the gate is close to orthogonal to the accrual leg being tested, reducing the endogeneity that afflicts book-equity and earnings gates.

considered.name: LeveredIncomeIncreasingAccrualTrap
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Leverage does not make good accounting better, it makes bad accounting dangerous: only income-increasing accruals create a future reversal that must be absorbed while debt service continues, so among cheap firms the penalty for accrual-dependent earnings should scale with debt intensity and be switched off entirely for firms reporting conservative, income-decreasing accruals.
considered.reasoning: The asymmetry the critic identified is now explicit in the expression: INDICATOR keeps only the positive part of accruals, so firms with income-decreasing accruals receive a penalty of exactly zero regardless of leverage and no highly levered firm can be pushed into the long leg by its debt alone, which also removes the leverage main effect from the long side. Using the cross-sectional rank of debt intensity rather than its raw level prevents a handful of extremely levered firms from dominating the standardized leg while preserving the ordering that the amplification hypothesis requires.

considered.name: RevenueGatedIncomeIncreasingAccrualOnly
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Only income-increasing accruals create an obligation to reverse; income-decreasing accruals are conservatism and should earn no reward, so among firms cheap on revenue the short leg should be built purely from those inflating current earnings while the long leg holds all firms with no accrual inflation.
considered.reasoning: The levered asymmetric penalty produced the strongest cross-sectional slope in the entire archive (FMB 3.37) but a negative alpha, which localizes the problem in the leverage multiplier's low-leverage factor tilt rather than in the asymmetry; removing leverage and keeping the positive-part restriction should retain the slope while restoring the enterprise gate's alpha. It also directly tests whether the accrual side of the value-trap story is one-sided, a question the symmetric legs cannot answer.

considered.name: WorkingCapitalChargedEnterpriseYield
considered.expression: RATIO(SUB(ebitda, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))
considered.hypothesis: The correct enterprise multiple charges operating profit for the working capital the business had to absorb to produce it, so a firm is cheap only if the profit remaining after that charge is large relative to total enterprise value.
considered.reasoning: Every enterprise-gated signal in the archive uses a [0,1] rank gate that flattens most of the cross-section and has repeatedly produced FMB t-stats of 0.3–2.6, whereas the archive's continuous-scale signals reliably delivered FMB t-stats above 3 but only ever used equity-market deflators, which are HML-collinear. This construction is continuous *and* enterprise-scaled, embedding the accrual correction in the numerator, so it is the natural test of whether the FMB weakness of the winning family is caused by the gate's functional form rather than its economics.

considered.name: EnterpriseYieldGatedDepreciationAdequacy
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(dp, at))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The EBITDA multiple's specific blind spot is that it ignores capital consumption, so for firms that look cheap on EBITDA the decisive accounting question is depreciation adequacy: a peer-abnormally high depreciation charge means the profit being capitalized will never reach shareholders, making the apparent cheapness an artifact of the multiple's construction.
considered.reasoning: This is not a normalization swap but a new claim about *which* accrual matters for *which* multiple: depreciation is the largest non-cash charge and is precisely the item the enterprise gate excludes, so pairing them tests a mechanism no archived signal addresses. Note the sign is deliberately the opposite of the archived DepreciationConservatismValue, where high depreciation was rewarded because net income was already charged for it — the reversal is forced by the gate's construction, which makes the two results jointly interpretable rather than redundant.

considered.name: RevenueGatedCollectionEfficiencyDecay
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(TREND(RATIO(SUB(act, che), sale), 5)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A single year's accrual build-up is mostly cyclical noise, but a multi-year upward drift in receivables-and-inventory per dollar of revenue is evidence of structural decay — lengthening collection periods and slower inventory turns — and a firm cheap on revenue with decaying collection efficiency is a business in decline rather than a mispriced asset.
considered.reasoning: The archive has tested accrual levels, one-year changes, three-year means, five-year volatility, five-year own-history rank and distance-from-peak, but never a fitted multi-year *slope*, which is the only statistic that distinguishes persistent directional deterioration from mean-reverting fluctuation. The economic claim is new and specific to the revenue-multiple gate: cheapness on revenue is only a bargain if that revenue is still being converted to cash at a stable or improving rate.

considered.name: RevenueGatedAccrualWithoutCashBuffer
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), 0)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(che, at))))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: An accrual reversal is an accounting event for a cash-rich firm but a financing event for a cash-poor one, because the unwind of receivables and inventory has to be funded; the value trap is therefore the joint state of cheap price, income-increasing accruals, and no liquidity buffer to absorb the reversal.
considered.reasoning: This adds a genuinely new conditioning dimension — the balance-sheet liquidity cushion — rather than another deflator, and it is deliberately built to avoid the failure of the earlier leverage-weighted version: the INDICATOR restricts amplification to income-increasing accruals, so a cash-poor firm with conservative accruals receives exactly zero penalty and cannot enter the long leg on liquidity grounds alone. Using the cross-sectional rank of cash scarcity keeps the weight bounded in [0,1] so a few cash-hoarding firms cannot dominate the standardized leg.

considered.name: RevenueGatedUnjustifiedWorkingCapitalInvestment
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(SUB(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), at), MUL(GROWTH(sale, 1), LAG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), at), 1)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Working capital should grow in proportion to revenue, so the benchmark for normal accrual investment is last year's working-capital intensity scaled by this year's revenue growth; only the excess over that benchmark represents receivables and inventory accumulating without corresponding business expansion, which is the accounting signature of a value trap.
considered.reasoning: This implements an explicit expectation model for normal accruals — the symbolic analogue of the Jones-model fitted value — instead of the crude industry demeaning that made the earlier discretionary-accrual attempt fail (alpha 0.2%, t 0.14), and it is continuous with no degenerate mass point. It also sharpens the interaction with the revenue-multiple gate: a firm cheap on revenue that is investing in working capital faster than its revenue justifies is exactly the case where cheapness reflects deteriorating fundamentals rather than mispricing.

considered.name: RevenueGatedPureWorkingCapitalAccrual
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), at)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The value-trap mechanism is about working capital — receivables and inventory accumulating without cash — and depreciation belongs to capital intensity rather than earnings manipulation, so removing the depreciation term should leave the economically relevant accrual signal intact.
considered.reasoning: This is the exact complement of Signal 1: together they partition the champion's leg into its depreciation and working-capital components under an unchanged gate, so whichever carries the +4.4% alpha and the 2.48 slope is identified rather than inferred. The distinction matters economically because a depreciation-driven result is a capital-intensity/conservatism story while a working-capital-driven result is the accrual-quality story this project is about.

considered.name: RevenueGatedWorkingCapitalRelease
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(MUL(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 0))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The abnormal return in cheap stocks comes from firms actively liquidating working capital into cash — collections improving, inventories clearing — a self-help operational turn the market underprices, whereas the absence of accrual inflation by itself is not rewarded.
considered.reasoning: This is the mirror image of the positive-part tests whose slopes were the archive's strongest but whose alphas were negative, which logically locates the champion's abnormal return in the negative-accrual tail; scoring only the magnitude of working-capital *releases* tests that inference directly. If it delivers alpha comparable to the champion with a positive slope, the economic story sharpens from "avoid accrual-inflated cheap firms" to "buy cheap firms converting working capital into cash."

considered.name: CashCollectedRevenueToEnterprise
considered.expression: RATIO(SUB(sale, DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1)), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))
considered.hypothesis: The right revenue multiple charges revenue for the portion that was not collected but instead parked in receivables and inventory, so cash-collected revenue per dollar of enterprise value is the accrual-proof version of the sales multiple.
considered.reasoning: The continuous-form test so far charged *EBITDA* for working capital, which turned it into a cash-flow yield that FF5 spans (alpha −1.9% despite FMB 3.11); applying the same correction to the revenue line instead keeps the signal a top-line multiple, which is a different factor exposure profile and matches the gate that has worked best. It also preserves a continuous, well-spread scale, addressing the persistent FMB weakness of the rank-gated family without reverting to a profit-based cash-flow yield.

considered.name: RevenueGatedCashShareConversion
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(che, act), 1), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Collection is directly observable as a shift in the composition of current assets: when cash rises as a share of current assets, receivables and inventory are being converted into money, and a cheap firm showing that shift is realizing the value its balance sheet claims rather than accumulating paper claims.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the depreciation channel entirely, along with its sign-fitting problem, and replaces it with a conversion-event mechanism: taking the *change* in the cash share removes the static industry and size differences that made the level version of che/act uninformative, leaving only the year-over-year liquidity transformation. It is also a scale-free composition measure requiring no deflator choice, so it is not a variant of any asset-scaled accrual leg in the archive, and coverage should be high since only act and che are needed over two years.

considered.name: RevenueGatedOwnScaleAccrualSurprise
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at), MA(ABS(RATIO(SUB(SUB(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), DELTA(SUB(SUB(lct, dlc), txp), 1)), dp), at)), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A given accrual is only informative relative to how large that firm's accruals normally are: a distributor whose working capital routinely swings by five percent of assets is not manipulating earnings when it does so again, while the same swing at a firm that normally reports negligible accruals is a genuine anomaly.
considered.reasoning: Rather than averaging two correlated horizons, this uses the firm's own three-year mean absolute accrual as the *scaling* denominator, converting the cross-sectional accrual level into a firm-specific standardized surprise — the only construction in the archive where the accrual is normalized by its own dispersion rather than by a balance-sheet or income deflator. The denominator is an absolute value so it cannot invert the sign, and the mechanism is economically distinct from the earlier difference-from-mean surprise because it identifies unusual accrual *magnitude relative to habitual volatility*, which is what separates opportunistic reporting from ordinary business-model variation.

considered.name: RevenueGatedAccrualPerUnitOperatingProfit
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful measure of accrual reliance is how much working-capital investment the firm absorbed per dollar of the operating profit it habitually earns; when a year's working-capital build-up rivals the firm's normal profit, the reported earnings have no cash counterpart.
considered.reasoning: The sign-inversion defect is repaired exactly where the critic located it: the deflator is now the three-year mean of absolute operating profit, which is strictly positive so loss-making firms can no longer be scored as clean, and the smoothing prevents a single near-zero EBITDA year from exploding the ratio. Deflating by earnings power rather than by assets or sales is the one scaling the archive has never tested with a stable denominator, and it is the most literal statement of the project's premise that earnings quality is about the cash backing of profit.

considered.name: NormalizedEarningsPowerGateAccrual
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(ebitda, 3), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness should be judged against normalized rather than spot profitability, because a single depressed or inflated EBITDA year misclassifies cyclical firms; a firm trading cheaply relative to its three-year average operating profit is genuinely cheap, and that is the population where accrual quality decides the outcome.
considered.reasoning: Both the current champion and its predecessor use spot multiples in the gate while the winning accrual leg uses smoothed earnings power, an internal inconsistency worth resolving: normalizing the gate the same way makes the conditioning variable measure durable cheapness rather than a one-year earnings dip. This is a change to the economic definition of the gate rather than a denominator tweak, and if it lifts both the slope and the alpha it tells us the champion has been partly conditioning on cyclical noise.

considered.name: AssetSideAccrualPerEarningsPower
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The trap mechanism is revenue booked but not collected and goods produced but not sold, so the asset side of working capital alone should carry the signal, while operating liabilities reflect supplier financing that is not an earnings-quality problem.
considered.reasoning: Under an asset deflator and a book-to-market gate, the asset-side-only leg earned little alpha (1.0%, t 1.06) while the netted version earned 2.5%, but that test predates both the revenue gate and the earnings-power deflator, so the decomposition needs to be redone in the winning configuration before the final round. It also tests directly whether the liability side belongs in the measure — the question the gross-churn inversion first raised and no configuration has resolved cleanly.

considered.name: ProfitDestinationCashVersusWorkingCapital
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(dvc, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Profit has to go somewhere, and where it goes reveals whether it was real: a cheap firm that sends earnings to shareholders as cash dividends has demonstrably converted profit into money, whereas one whose earnings disappear into growing receivables and inventory has not, so the net flow of profit toward owners versus toward working capital is the sharpest earnings-quality test available.
considered.reasoning: This is a new mechanism rather than another deflator: it places a hard cash outflow (dividends) and a soft accrual absorption on the same earnings-power scale and takes their difference, so it measures the *destination* of profit instead of only its accrual content. Because dividends and working-capital investment are largely independent decisions, the combined leg should carry information beyond the champion's accrual-only measure, and the dividend-gated test already showed the payout channel is informative (alpha 3.4%, t 3.20) without contaminating the gate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SupplierCreditPerEarningsPower
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(lct, dlc), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Growth in operating liabilities is not an earnings-quality defect but interest-free financing extended by suppliers and employees to firms they expect to survive, so among cheap firms an expanding operating-liability base relative to earnings power signals bargaining power and funding relief rather than accrual inflation.
considered.reasoning: This completes the decomposition begun by the accepted asset-side test: the two proposals together partition the champion's netted accrual leg under the winning gate and deflator, and the sign here is deliberately *unnegated*, which makes it a falsifiable economic claim rather than a smoothing tweak. The archive already produced indirect evidence for it — penalizing operating-liability growth with the same sign as asset growth inverted the alpha from +2.5% to −2.3% — but the liability side has never been tested on its own, so this establishes whether Sloan's netting is genuinely required or whether the asset side is doing all the work.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalStockPerEarningsPower
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: A business that must keep several years' worth of operating profit permanently locked in receivables and inventory has a structurally poor claim on its own book value, because that capital is illiquid and impairable; a cheap firm with a light working-capital stock relative to its earnings power owns assets it can actually monetize.
considered.reasoning: This is the *level*, not any difference, so it cannot telescope into the flow measure the critic identified, and it resolves the stock-versus-flow question in the winning configuration: the bloat level previously earned alpha of +3.4% but no cross-sectional slope under an asset deflator and a book-to-market gate, and the untested question is whether the earnings-power deflator supplies the missing slope by turning capital intensity into an interpretable "years of profit tied up" quantity. Because it needs no differencing, coverage should be at or above the champion's 0.110.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DebtFundedWorkingCapitalAbsorption
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The dangerous configuration is not accrual absorption alone but accrual absorption financed by short-term borrowing: when a cheap firm's profit disappears into receivables and inventory while its current debt simultaneously expands relative to earnings power, the working-capital cycle is being funded by lenders who can withdraw, which is the standard pre-distress sequence.
considered.reasoning: This asks a new economic question — the *funding source* of the accrual, measured as a flow of short-term credit — rather than reweighting tails of an existing leg to chase in-sample statistics, and it differs from the earlier cash-buffer and total-leverage tests, which used stock-based scarcity or debt-intensity multipliers rather than the contemporaneous change in current debt. Both components are placed on the same earnings-power scale so their sum is interpretable as "profit absorbed plus short-term credit drawn, per dollar of normal profit," and the leg stays continuous with no censoring or point mass.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AssetBuildupAndShortTermDebtDraw
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(act, che), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The trap configuration is uncollected revenue and unsold inventory financed by short-term borrowing; growth in other operating liabilities should get no credit at all, because supplier and accrued liabilities are as much a symptom of strain as a source of free financing.
considered.reasoning: The winning leg algebraically credits total current-liability growth while double-penalizing current debt, and the standalone liability test produced a wrong-signed slope (FMB −2.445), so the coherent version penalizes asset-side absorption and debt draw and credits neither. This isolates whether the champion's strength survives removal of the liability-reward term, which is the last unresolved sign question in the leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TotalDebtFundedWorkingCapitalAbsorption
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: What matters is that the working-capital cycle is being financed by creditors rather than by operations, and long-term borrowing funds the same absorption as short-term borrowing while merely postponing the refinancing date.
considered.reasoning: The short-term-debt version delivered the archive's best joint result, so the immediate question is whether the mechanism is about rollover risk specifically or about creditor funding of accruals generally; using total debt issuance answers it in one test. If total debt performs as well, the economic story broadens from a liquidity-timing story to an external-financing story, and if it performs worse the maturity structure is essential.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WorkingCapitalAbsorptionWithRolloverExposure
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(dlc, MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The danger is the standing stock of debt that must be refinanced within a year measured against normal profit, not merely this year's incremental draw: a cheap firm absorbing profit into working capital while carrying several years of earnings power in current debt has no margin for the reversal.
considered.reasoning: Substituting the level of current debt for its change tests state versus flow in the funding dimension, the same distinction that mattered on the accrual side, and levels are far more persistent than annual changes, so if the state version holds up it should lower turnover and stabilize portfolio composition further. It also guards against the possibility that the champion's Δdlc term is picking up transitory financing noise rather than genuine rollover exposure.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NormalizedGateDebtFundedAbsorption
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MA(ebitda, 3), SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(ADD(RATIO(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), RATIO(DELTA(dlc, 1), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness should be judged against normalized earnings power rather than a single year's revenue, so the firms in which the funding-augmented accrual test bites hardest are those trading cheaply relative to the profit they can sustain through a cycle.
considered.reasoning: The two best-performing design choices of generation 8 were the funding-augmented leg (Sharpe 0.553) and the smoothed earnings-power gate (alpha 4.1%, t 3.84), and they have never been combined; since the leg's deflator is already three-year mean profit, this also makes the gate and leg internally consistent in what they treat as earnings power. It is a deliberate final-round consolidation, and its value is that it either confirms the revenue gate is doing something the profit gate cannot, or delivers the strongest configuration in the archive.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProfitUsesIdentityPerEarningsPower
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(SUB(dvc, DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1)), DELTA(dlc, 1)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3)), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: Earnings quality is fully described by where the profit went: cash paid to owners is proof of conversion, profit absorbed into receivables and inventory is unproven, and short-term credit drawn is proof that the profit never arrived — the net of these three, scaled by normal profit, is the complete test of whether a cheap firm's earnings are real.
considered.reasoning: This is a single accounting identity rather than a weighted blend of standardized legs: the dividend and absorption terms already earned +3.1% (t 3.34) and the absorption-plus-debt terms +3.8% (t 4.30), and they describe complementary uses of the same profit, so combining them within one ratio imposes economic rather than statistical weights. It is the most complete statement of the project's premise — that value is trustworthy only when reported profit shows up as cash — and it is the natural signal to carry forward if it holds both the slope and the alpha.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AbsorptionVersusFundsFromOperations
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(NEG(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(SUB(SUB(act, che), SUB(lct, dlc)), 1), ADD(ib, dp)), MA(ABS(ebitda), 3))), 1)))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful funding test is whether the working capital a firm absorbed this year was covered by the funds its operations actually generated — net income plus the depreciation add-back — because when absorption exceeds funds from operations the firm must go to creditors or shareholders, and a cheap firm in that position is a trap regardless of what its income statement says.
considered.reasoning: This replaces Δche, which as noted is a residual of operating, investing and financing flows and duplicates the cash term already netted inside working capital, with funds from operations (ib + dp), the standard internal-funding measure and one that is broadly populated so coverage stays near 0.110 rather than dropping to cash-flow-statement levels. It is the internal-funding complement to the archive's winning external-funding term: that signal asks whether creditors financed the accrual, this asks whether operations could have, and both are expressed per unit of normal earnings power so the magnitudes are interpretable.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: Internally consistent and correctly signed, but it is a plain additive stack of two of the most heavily documented anomalies (book-to-market and Sloan total accruals), i.e. a textbook "value + earnings quality" composite with no genuinely new mechanism.

This is a cosmetic functional-form variant of CashBackedBookToMarket (MIN instead of SUM of the identical two ranks), and the MIN operator discards ordering information in the short leg by pooling expensive-clean firms with cheap-dirty firms into an indistinguishable low bucket.

Same two ingredients again, and the multiplicative construction is internally broken for negative-book-equity firms (a negative BM times a *high* accrual-quality weight becomes *more* negative, so good accounting quality perversely lowers the score), while the declared INTERACTION_TYPE "ratio" contradicts an expression that is a product.

The EBITDA/EV plus balance-sheet working-capital-accrual pairing is the most defensible construction in this batch and is capital-structure neutral rather than another BM-plus-Sloan restatement, though the enterprise-value denominator can go negative or near-zero for net-cash firms and should be guarded before the rank.

The hypothesis is about *revenue* cash conversion but the expression adds apalch, so a firm that simply stretches its payables (a distress rather than revenue-quality signal) scores as high-quality, and recch/invch/apalch have notoriously sparse and sign-convention-inconsistent coverage that will distort the sort.

The second-moment accrual-opacity leg is a substantively different mechanism from the level-based accrual anomaly and its interaction with cheapness is genuinely under-tested, but it partly rediscovers the known earnings/accrual-volatility effect and VOL(...,5) on forward-filled annual fundamentals must be verified to span five distinct fiscal years rather than five months.

The multiplicative conditioning is internally consistent (cheap-and-clean long, cheap-and-dirty short, expensive firms parked near zero) and structurally distinct from the archive's additive composites, but the underlying ingredients are textbook Sloan balance-sheet accruals crossed with value — a combination close to the published "accruals are stronger in value stocks / Piotroski-style value-trap" results, so the marginal novelty is limited.

The stated justification is internally false — the expression expands exactly to B/M minus NOWC/price, i.e. a fixed-weight linear function of standard book-to-market and another price-scaled ratio, so the claim that it "is not a linear function of standard book-to-market" and should escape HML is unsupported, and stripping working capital from book equity makes the negative-numerator (distress) tail more common and uninterpretable.

(EBITDA − depreciation − ΔNOWC)/market cap is a reconstruction of operating cash flow to price, i.e. a direct rediscovery of the long-published cash-flow-to-price value anomaly (Lakonishok-Shleifer-Vishny), with the only innovation being the data source for the same quantity.

The hypothesis and the expression disagree in sign logic — a rise in taxes *payable* means tax has been accrued but not remitted (a current-liability accrual that raises Sloan accruals), not that income was cash-confirmed; genuine tax confirmation requires cash taxes paid or the book-tax difference (Lev-Nissim), and Δtxp/at is additionally a tiny, mean-reverting, sparsely populated item that will contribute mostly noise at 50% SUMRANK weight.

It uses raw wcap (which includes che) rather than the archive's cash-excluded version, so a firm building cash gets penalized as "accrual-laden," directly contradicting the stated revenue-to-cash-conversion mechanism, and beyond that it is an admitted horizon variant (1-year change → 5-year trend) of an existing archive signal with worse coverage.

The information-risk/opacity channel is a legitimately different mechanism from the archive's accrual-level composites and the sign direction is coherent, but VOL over five annual observations is a very noisy second moment, wcap includes cash so part of what is measured is cash-holding variability rather than accounting opacity, and cheap-plus-stable risks collapsing into a generic quality-value tilt.

It uses exactly the same two ingredients and functional form as the archive's ValueConditionedBalanceSheetAccrual with the gate/direction roles permuted, which is close to a variant but does produce a genuinely different long-short composition (cheap-clean vs expensive-clean) and answers a well-posed attribution question, so it is worth one test but should not spawn further permutations.

The earnings-deflated accrual leg is essentially the published "percent accruals" measure (Hafzalla, Lundholm, Van Winkle), so novelty rests only on the earnings-yield gating, and the ABS(ib) denominator will be explosive for near-zero-earnings firms even after winsorization — but the sign logic is internally consistent and the deflator comparison against the gen-1 winner is a legitimate design test.

TS_SUM of annual DELTAs telescopes into a plain five-year level change (so the "stock vs flow" novelty claim is vacuous), and dividing a fundamental quantity by market cap makes the signal dominated by the 1/price denominator, i.e. a repackaged value/accrual-to-price ratio rather than a genuine value-accrual interaction.

This is a standard industry-demeaning of the archive's gen-1 winner with no new economic content, and dropping the WINSOR from the z-scored accrual leg leaves it more outlier-exposed than the original, so any Sharpe gain would be a cosmetic robustness result rather than an advance in mechanism.

A clearly motivated decomposition test that deliberately breaks Sloan's netting (asset and liability buildup entering with the same sign) with a sales deflator that is commensurate across both components; the sign structure matches the hypothesis and the economic claim about payables stretching is contestable but genuinely testable.

Replacing a noisy five-point volatility with a persistence count of income-decreasing-accrual years is a substantive, well-diagnosed repair of the failed ValueWithStableWorkingCapital rather than a cosmetic variant, though the 0–5 integer signal discards magnitude information and requires six years of annual data, so watch coverage and coarse-tercile instability.

The expression correctly implements Hribar–Collins cash-flow-statement accruals (ib+dpc−oancf, matching the depreciation-adjusted balance-sheet construct it replaces) inside the value gate that the archive shows is required for alpha, making it a substantive measurement upgrade rather than a cosmetic variant — though oancf availability will cut coverage and the accrual anomaly itself is of course published.

A legitimate and interpretable decomposition of the netted accrual leg, but the motivating inference is shaky (the gross-churn test also changed the deflator from `at` to `sale`, so the sign flip is confounded) and the result is largely predictable from the fact that the net measure already loads the liability side with the opposite sign.

This is a mechanical re-blend of two already-archived signals with no new economic content — the value term appears twice and the outcome is almost guaranteed to land between the additive and gated results, which diagnoses nothing beyond the known distributional artifact.

Magnitude-preserving three-year averaging is the right repair for the failed 0–5 persistence count and is internally consistent, but a 3-year mean of annual accrual ratios is close to a lower-frequency version of the same flow, so the informational gain over the one-year gated signal is likely modest.

Testing the accrual *stock* embedded in book equity rather than the annual flow is the most conceptually distinct proposal here, but the claim that it "never creates negative or uninterpretable" values is wrong — `ceq` can be small or negative and NOWC can be negative, so the ratio is unstable in exactly the distressed value tail that drives the effect, and it risks proxying for working-capital-intensive industries.

A single-operator deflator ablation, but the diagnosis is specific and credible (ABS(ib) explodes near zero earnings, plausibly explaining the 2.8-alpha / 1.4-FMB divergence) and the sales deflator is well-behaved, so the test is cheap and interpretable even if the economic novelty is thin.

The first term is the canonical Sloan/Hribar-Collins cash-flow accrual anomaly in its standard form and the second term is verbatim the already-archived CashFlowStatementAccrualGatedValue, so the "signal" is a mechanical union of a published anomaly and a tested expression rather than a new mechanism, and the diluted product term will likely just drag the level-effect's own alpha toward the accrual main effect.

The sign convention for recch/invch (cash-flow effect, positive on release) is correctly reasoned and the asset-side-only, cash-flow-measured leg is a substantive measurement change motivated by two diagnosed archive results, though it remains the same B/M-times-z-score gate architecture whose Sharpe has repeatedly collapsed and recch/invch availability is patchy enough to threaten coverage and leg stability.

This is a denominator swap on the already-tested SoftBookShareGatedValue idea and, stripped of framing, is simply value crossed with cash holdings — a well-documented published combination — while che/act mostly sorts on industry and size rather than on accrual reliability.

Replacing fragile ceq scaling with total assets and demeaning within industry is a defensible, diagnosis-driven fix to the SoftBookShare failure and tests the stock-versus-flow question the archive left unresolved, but it is still a normalization variant of an archived signal within the same gated family, so the incremental information is modest.

The HML-collinearity diagnosis is the sharpest reasoning in this batch and swapping the gate to the archive's best raw-return valuation leg is a genuinely different experiment, though the standard Sloan accrual leg is unchanged and EBITDA/EV is unstable when enterprise value approaches or crosses zero for net-cash firms.

The MIN construction is internally consistent and preserves a continuous yield scale, but note it algebraically reduces to earnings yield minus the positive part of (approximately) total accruals — i.e. the archived EarningsYieldAsymmetricAccrualPenalty re-expressed in levels rather than ranks — so its novelty rests entirely on the scaling change and cash-flow-statement measurement, and unwinsorized raw yields will let a few outliers dominate the Fama-MacBeth slope.

A legitimate but incremental recombination of two archive parents (EV-yield gate × cash-flow-statement accrual leg) with a coherent hypothesis-to-expression mapping, though the ~0.09 coverage from `oancf` and the prior weak FMB slope of the CF-accrual leg under a B/M gate temper expectations that it will dominate both parents.

This is a one-operator denominator tweak (dropping `che`) of the archive's existing EVYieldGatedAccrualQuality with an otherwise identical accrual leg — a cosmetic robustness variant rather than a substantively different mechanism, and since RANK already neutralizes extreme-but-positive EV ratios the fix only matters for the small subset with negative enterprise value.

Another gate-swap recombination of archive legs, but the FMB-versus-alpha diagnostic motivating it is honest and specific; note the INDICATOR creates a large point mass at zero (all firms without a prior build-up), so the ZSCORE and resulting sort will be driven by a degenerate spike that should be checked for portfolio-composition instability.

The hypothesis is asymmetric (leverage makes an accrual *reversal* existential) but the expression multiplies symmetrically, so highly levered firms with income-*decreasing* accruals are scored as the most attractive long positions — an implication the reasoning never defends — and the product embeds a leverage main effect that is itself confounded with distress and value.

The argument that every gate tested so far has an accrual-contaminated numerator is a genuine and non-obvious critique, and a cash-distribution gate is economically distinct from the archive's book/earnings/EBITDA gates; the main risk is that `dvc`=0 for non-payers produces a large tied rank block that turns the composite into a scaled pure-accrual signal over half the cross-section, and that payers skew large-cap where the accrual effect is weakest.

The stock-versus-flow diagnostic is well-posed and the MIN double hurdle is a structurally new combiner rather than another deflator, but the two legs are mechanically related (the flow is essentially a difference of the stock) and MIN discards the magnitude of the passing leg, so it may simply inherit whichever component is noisier rather than combining their complementary strengths.

This is a one-operator normalization swap (RANK → IND_RANK) on the archive's existing best signal SalesToEnterpriseGatedAccrualQuality, and while industry-neutralizing a margin-driven revenue multiple is economically sensible, it is the kind of cosmetic variant the objective explicitly discourages absent a diagnosed failure it repairs.

Averaging the two enterprise-yield gates from two already-evaluated signals against an identical accrual leg is an ensemble of prior results rather than a new mechanism, and since sale/EV and ebitda/EV share the same denominator and are highly correlated, the outcome will almost mechanically interpolate between the two known alphas.

The positive-part restriction is a defensible decomposition test that isolates whether the negative alpha of LeveredIncomeIncreasingAccrualTrap came from the leverage multiplier or the asymmetry, and the expression's sign logic is coherent, though the hard indicator leaves roughly half the cross-section stacked at exactly zero — the same degeneracy this batch's own sixth proposal complains about.

Swapping the accrual deflator from assets to sales under the existing best gate is a single-parameter robustness variant whose "commensurate deflator" justification is rhetorical rather than economic — the gate's denominator is enterprise value, not sales, so nothing is actually made internally consistent — and the archive already shows this leg's behavior under a different gate.

This is the only proposal that changes functional form rather than a component, embedding the accrual charge in the numerator to produce a continuous enterprise-scaled yield, and it directly tests the stated diagnosis that the gated family's weak FMB slopes come from the flattened [0,1] rank gate — though the reviewer should note it sits close to published cash-flow-to-enterprise-value and cash-based-profitability measures, so a high-alpha result may be rediscovery rather than novelty.

The stated diagnosis is internally inconsistent — the INDICATOR was identical in both the book-to-market and enterprise-gated reversal signals, so it cannot explain an alpha difference that arose purely from changing the gate — and the smoothing itself is a functional-form tweak on an already-evaluated mechanism rather than a new economic claim.

This is essentially the sign-flipped, industry-unadjusted twin of the already-evaluated EnterpriseYieldGatedDepreciationAdequacy (whose fmb −3.36 is explicitly used to set the expected sign here rather than the stated hypothesis), so it is both a near-rediscovery and a case of fitting the sign to prior evidence, and dp/at is a well-known capital-intensity proxy that delivered essentially zero alpha in that earlier test.

Dropping the depreciation term from the champion's accrual leg is a small edit but an economically meaningful one (capital consumption versus working-capital manipulation), the expression matches the hypothesis and sign, and paired with a decomposition motivation it is a legitimate identification test rather than a cosmetic reshuffle — though the incremental information over SalesToEnterpriseGatedAccrualQuality may be modest.

The indicator logic correctly isolates the magnitude of working-capital releases and the sign is internally consistent, and it is the untested mirror of the already-evaluated positive-part variant motivated by a genuine slope/alpha divergence; the main risk is that roughly half the cross-section is censored to a single point mass, so the product with the rank gate may produce unstable portfolio composition rather than a clean conditional effect.

This is an equal-weight blend of two already-evaluated signals under an unchanged gate whose components (one-year Δ non-cash current assets and the five-year trend in non-cash current assets per sale) are measured off the same balance-sheet line and are therefore likely correlated, so it proposes no new mechanism and is the kind of averaging refinement that typically interpolates rather than improves.

The construction is coherent, continuous, and distinct from the archive's EBITDA-charged enterprise yield, but Δ(act−che) is typically only a few percent of sales, so the signal risks being near-collinear with the plain sales-to-enterprise multiple — a known value anomaly — and the review should require evidence that the working-capital charge adds anything beyond the base multiple.

Deflating ΔNOWC by signed EBITDA is internally inconsistent: for negative-EBITDA firms the ratio flips sign, so a firm bleeding cash into receivables while losing money is scored as *clean*, and 1% winsorization suppresses outliers but does not repair the sign inversion — the archive's use of ABS(ib) in PercentAccrualGatedEarningsYield shows the fix was already known.

This is a three-year moving average bolted onto the champion's accrual leg — a smoothing tweak whose economic content (chronic vs. transitory accrual reliance) was already tested in the archive as ChronicAccrualRelianceGatedValue, which underperformed the one-year version under its own gate, so the expected information gain is thin and largely cosmetic.

The stated distinction from Proposal 1 is false — NWC_t − NWC_{t−3} is exactly the telescoped sum of the three annual deltas the reasoning claims it is not, so up to a factor of three and the timing of a slow-moving deflator this is the same variable as ChronicAccrualPerEarningsPower and the pair cannot discriminate "persistence" from "accumulated overhang."

Normalizing the valuation gate with three-year average EBITDA to match the smoothed deflator in the accrual leg is a coherent and internally consistent change to the definition of cheapness rather than a denominator tweak, though it remains a modest step from the already-tested spot EV-yield gate and inherits the sign ambiguity of RANK over firms with negative average EBITDA.

A clean, well-motivated ablation that isolates the asset side under the winning gate/deflator and directly addresses an unresolved question raised by the gross-churn inversion, but prior evidence (asset-side 1.0%/t 1.06 vs. netted 2.5%) makes a downgrade the likeliest outcome, so its value is diagnostic rather than performance-seeking.

Placing a hard cash outflow and a soft accrual absorption on the same earnings-power scale is a genuinely new mechanism with a sign that matches the expression's natural direction, though the reviewer should note that dvc is zero for a large fraction of firms — so the signal degenerates to the champion's accrual leg for non-payers and effectively adds a known payout-ratio effect for payers, which must be controlled for when interpreting any improvement.

This is explicitly constructed to graft the FMB slope of one prior specification onto the alpha of another using the same in-sample evaluation statistics, which is metric-mining rather than an economic hypothesis; the arbitrary relative weighting of two separately z-scored legs and the mislabeled "avoids the point mass" claim (the extra term is identically zero for all buildup firms) compound the problem.

A legitimate and internally consistent ablation of the champion leg — it removes the algebraically implicit reward for operating-liability growth and the accidental double-penalty on Δdlc — but it is an incremental component swap combining two already-tested archive terms rather than a new mechanism, and the asset-side-only leg previously produced a null alpha on its own.

Clean one-variable test of maturity structure versus creditor funding generally, but note that Δ(dltt+dlc) scaled by earnings power moves this leg toward the published net-debt-issuance / external-financing anomaly, so a strong result would need to be shown incremental to plain debt issuance rather than treated as a new earnings-quality finding.

The state-versus-flow question is fair, but dlc/MA|ebitda| is a level with far larger cross-sectional dispersion than ΔNWC and will likely dominate the leg, turning the signal into a value-plus-short-term-leverage/distress composite that is both a known construct and partly redundant with the EV-based gate (which already penalizes debt in its denominator).

Filling the untested cell formed by the archive's two best components is defensible and the gate/leg deflator consistency argument is genuine, but it is close to a cosmetic recombination whose outcome is largely predictable from the two parent results.

The hypothesis is about working-capital expansion "funded out of genuine operating cash," but the expression uses Δche, a residual of operating, investing, financing and payout flows (and one that enters with an inflated double weight given ΔNWC already nets cash out), so what it computes is a cash-hoarding tilt rather than the stated self-funding mechanism.

The economically-weighted single-ratio combination of two independently supported terms is a reasonable and untested construction, but the "complete accounting identity" claim is overstated (capex, equity issuance and long-term debt are omitted) and the dvc term will impose a dividend-payer tilt that must be shown incremental to payout-based predictors.
